newsitem.title: SPAIN: Two million protesters take to streets in Spain.
newsitem.headline: Two million protesters take to streets in Spain.

text.p: More than two million people took to the streets across Spain on Monday night to mourn the death of a young politician and angrily condemn the Basque separatist guerrillas who killed him.

Only hours after 29-year-old Miguel Angel Blanco was laid to rest in his home town of Ermua, Spaniards in record numbers mounted massive demonstrations in Madrid, Barcelona and other cities to vent their fury and grief.
While most of the gatherings were peaceful, the public backlash against the rebel group ETA turned violent in the Basque country late on Monday.

In San Sebastian, hundreds of anti-ETA protesters hurled eggs and rocks at offices and a bar used by the rebels' political wing, Herri Batasuna. The people inside retaliated with Molotov cocktails, police said. At least two people were reported injured. Similar incidents took place in Bilbao.

King Juan Carlos, in a rare televised address to the nation, praised the Spanish people for their "condemnation of terrorism" and urged them to "continue fighting in this endless struggle for democracy, liberty and human rights".
"The death of Miguel Angel has not been in vain," the king declared from the lawn of the royal palace.

ETA guerrillas abducted Blanco, a Basque town councillor, on Thursday and threatened to execute him in 48 hours unless 500 rebel inmates were moved to prisons in the Basque region. The government refused, and rebels shot him just after the deadline passed.
Blanco was found on Saturday dumped on a mountain roadside outside the Basque city of San Sebastian, his hands tied behind his back and two bullets in his brain. He died 12 hours later.

In central Madrid on Monday night, Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar led a procession of hundreds of political leaders, bearing a huge banner that read "Peace, Unity and Freedom." A sea of protesters stretching for several kilometres chanted "Murderers! Murderers!".
"They are sons of bitches, all of ETA," one man yelled.

Blanco, whose death has unified Spaniards in outrage against the guerrillas, was buried earlier on Monday in Ermua in the heart of the Basque country in a sombre ceremony that brought the country briefly to a standstill.
Millions stopped work at noon to observe 10 minutes' silence. Traffic came to a halt. Flights out of Madrid's international airport stopped.

In Ermua, where Blanco was a popular politician and an accountant by trade, tens of thousands lined the streets outside the packed chapel where Aznar and Crown Prince Felipe comforted grieving family members.

Choking back tears, Blanco's 23-year-old girlfriend, Maria del Mar Diaz, placed a pair of drumsticks atop the dark wooden casket before it was sealed inside the burial vault at the town cemetery. Blanco played drums in a local band.
"With the barbarous assassination of Miguel Angel, terrorism has shown its face cold and filled with cruelty," Bishop Ricardo Blazquez told mourners at Blanco's funeral.
"There is no justification for the murder of an innocent," he said of Blanco, a low-ranking member of Spain's ruling party.
As the national day of mourning turned to night, residents of Madrid and Barcelona mounted what the state-run media described as the biggest demonstrations in Spanish history.

Authorities said 1.5 million people turned out in Madrid and another million in Barcelona to protest against ETA, which has killed nearly 800 people in its 29-year struggle for an independent Basque homeland.
Reflecting the depth of public emotion, Spain's 59-year-old king addressed the nation in a taped interview with state television.

Juan Carlos, who tries to avoid getting involved in politics, sealed his position as guardian of Spanish democracy in 1981, when he made a stirring televised speech after military officers stormed Parliament and held legislators hostage in a failed coup attempt.
Aznar vowed earlier on Monday to intensify the fight against ETA. "We will put a stop to terrorism," he said.

Spain's top political leaders, after an urgent meeting, announced a break with Herri Batasuna "until ETA stops killing or until Herri Batasuna ruptures its alliances in the world of terror". The group holds two seats in the national congress and is also represented in the Basque and Navarre parliaments.
In official circles, the latest killing was seen as a sign of ETA's desperation and there was a fear that if cornered the group would respond with more attacks.

ETA violence has stirred public anger before, but it was the death sentence passed against such an innocent victim that cut to the heart of Spanish society. Pope John Paul and other world leaders have condemned the killing.
